title: Rational representations and coordinate Hopf comodules
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], let $G$ be an affine finite-type $k$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and let $A=k[G]$ with its coordinate Hopf maps $\Delta,\epsilon,S$ [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf]. For a $k$-vector space $V$ of arbitrary dimension, put $V_R=V\otimes_kR$ [def-weil-module-base-change]. A rational representation on $V$ means a family of group homomorphisms $r_R:G(R)\to\operatorname{Aut}_R(V_R)$ natural in commutative $k$-algebras $R$, where $G(R)=\operatorname{Hom}_{k\text{-alg}}(A,R)$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. These representations correspond bijectively to $k$-linear maps $c:V\to V\otimes_kA$ satisfying $(c\otimes1)c=(1\otimes\Delta)c$ and $(1\otimes\epsilon)c=1_V$. Explicitly, $r_R(x)(v\otimes b)=\sum_i v_i\otimes x(a_i)b$ when $c(v)=\sum_i v_i\otimes a_i$, and $c(v)=r_A(\mathrm{id}_A)(v\otimes1)$. A linear map $f:V\to W$ intertwines all these actions if and only if $(f\otimes1)c_V=c_Wf$. For finite-dimensional $V$ these natural representations are precisely homomorphisms of $k$-group schemes $G\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$, with $\operatorname{GL}(V)(R)=\operatorname{Aut}_R(V_R)$, as in [def-wf-algebraic-representations]. The trivial representation has coaction $v\mapsto v\otimes1$, and the tensor representation has coaction $v\otimes w\mapsto\sum_{i,j}(v_i\otimes w_j)\otimes a_ib_j$ if $c_V(v)=\sum_i v_i\otimes a_i$ and $c_W(w)=\sum_j w_j\otimes b_j$. Tensor products are universal for bilinear maps [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. All vector spaces lie in one fixed universe; families of such objects may lie in a containing universe.

source.place: Remark 4.1, equations (24)--(25), printed p.84; Chapter 4(a), printed p.83; tensor operations in Chapter 4(e), printed pp.87--88.

proof.text: Use the tensor universal property [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] throughout: pure tensors generate, so maps specified on them are unique. In particular the maps $(v\otimes a)\otimes b\leftrightarrow v\otimes(a\otimes b)$, $v\otimes t\mapsto tv$ for $t\in k$, and $a\otimes v\leftrightarrow v\otimes a$ give the associativity, unit and symmetry identifications; their inverse composites fix every pure tensor. By [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property], $A\otimes_kA$ is a commutative $k$-algebra with maps $\iota_1(a)=a\otimes1$, $\iota_2(a)=1\otimes a$, and for points $x,y:A\to R$ there is the algebra map $m_{x,y}(a\otimes b)=x(a)y(b)$. By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra], $G\times_kG=\operatorname{Spec}(A\otimes_kA)$ with projections $\operatorname{Spec}\iota_1,\operatorname{Spec}\iota_2$, so the pair $(x,y)$ is the point $m_{x,y}$ of $G\times_kG$ (it is the unique algebra map with $m_{x,y}\iota_1=x$, $m_{x,y}\iota_2=y$). Since the maps in [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf] are pullbacks of the given group operations, their pointwise formulas are $xy=m_{x,y}\Delta$, $e_R=u_R\epsilon$, and $x^{-1}=xS$. In particular $\iota_1\iota_2=\Delta$ as points of $G(A\otimes_kA)$, because $m_{\iota_1,\iota_2}$ is the identity.

source.place: Remark 4.1, printed p.84, multiplication calculation following (25); Proposition 3.5 for pointwise multiplication. Tensor identifications written explicitly.

proof.text:
Start with a natural family of $R$-linear endomorphisms $t_R(x)$ of $V_R$; for this step no group law is assumed. Set $d(v)=t_A(\mathrm{id}_A)(v\otimes1)$. This is $k$-linear. Naturality along the algebra map $x:A\to R$ says
$$(1\otimes x)t_A(\mathrm{id}_A)=t_R(x)(1\otimes x).$$
Applying it to $v\otimes1$ and using $R$-linearity gives $t_R(x)(v\otimes b)=b(1\otimes x)d(v)$. Thus $d$ determines every operator, since the $v\otimes b$ generate. Restriction to $v\otimes1$ and extension by $b$ are precisely [lem-weil-pbc-module-base-change-universal-property], after the symmetry identification of Step 1; [def-weil-module-base-change] specifies the scalar action. The maps $1\otimes x$ exist by the tensor universal property. This applies without a dimension bound on $V$.

source.place: Remark 4.1, printed p.84, universal element and restriction to a k-linear homomorphism.

proof.text:
Conversely, given any $k$-linear $d:V\to V\otimes_kA$, define $t_R(x)$ to be the unique $R$-linear extension of $(1\otimes x)d:V\to V_R$, using [lem-weil-pbc-module-base-change-universal-property] and Step 1. Hence for any finite presentation $d(v)=\sum_i v_i\otimes a_i$,
$$t_R(x)(v\otimes b)=\sum_i v_i\otimes x(a_i)b.$$
This formula is independent of the tensor presentation because it is the composite of the tensor map $1\otimes x$ and scalar multiplication, rather than a choice of presentation. For an algebra map $\alpha:R\to R'$, applying $1\otimes\alpha$ to the formula gives $\sum_i v_i\otimes\alpha(x(a_i))\alpha(b)$, which is $t_{R'}(\alpha x)(v\otimes\alpha(b))$. The equality extends to all tensors by generation. It proves naturality. At $R=A,x=\mathrm{id}_A,b=1$ the formula recovers $d$; Step 2 recovers $t$ from its restriction. Thus these constructions are inverse before imposing the group and comodule identities.

source.place: Remark 4.1, printed p.84, coaction-to-action formula and the finite sums in (25).

proof.text:
Now let $d=c$ be coassociative. For $c(v)=\sum_i v_i\otimes a_i$ and $c(v_i)=\sum_j v_{ij}\otimes a_{ij}$, coassociativity says
$$\sum_{i,j}v_{ij}\otimes a_{ij}\otimes a_i=\sum_i v_i\otimes\Delta(a_i).$$
Apply the linear map $v\otimes a\otimes b\mapsto v\otimes x(a)y(b)$, furnished by [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] and [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property]. By Step 3 its left side is $t_R(x)t_R(y)(v\otimes1)$; by Step 1 its right side is $t_R(xy)(v\otimes1)$. Both operators are $R$-linear, so agreement on $v\otimes1$ proves $t_R(xy)=t_R(x)t_R(y)$. Every displayed sum is finite for the particular vector in question; there is no uniform finite-basis assumption.

source.place: Remark 4.1, printed p.84, equations (24)-(25) and the computation of r(g1 g2).

proof.text: The counit identity gives $t_R(e_R)(v\otimes b)=\sum_i v_i\otimes u_R(\epsilon(a_i))b=v\otimes b$, using [def-weil-module-base-change] and the point formula $e_R=u_R\epsilon$ of Step 1. Thus $t_R(e_R)=1$. By Step 4, $t_R(x)t_R(xS)=t_R(xx^{-1})=1$ and $t_R(xS)t_R(x)=1$, since [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf] identifies $S$ with inversion. Consequently each $t_R(x)$ is an automorphism with inverse $t_R(xS)$. Together with Step 3 these are the required natural group homomorphisms $r_R$.

source.place: Remark 4.1, printed p.84, (24)-(25); inverse follows from the group law and the coordinate antipode.

proof.text:
For the reverse implication start with a representation $r$ and its $c$ from Step 2. Put $C=A\otimes_kA$ and take the two generic points $\iota_1,\iota_2:A\to C$ of Step 1. The formula of Step 2 gives
$$r_C(\iota_1)r_C(\iota_2)(v\otimes1)=\sum_{i,j}v_{ij}\otimes(a_{ij}\otimes a_i),$$
which identifies with $(c\otimes1)c(v)$ under Step 1. On the other hand the homomorphism law and $\iota_1\iota_2=\Delta$ give
$$r_C(\iota_1)r_C(\iota_2)(v\otimes1)=r_C(\Delta)(v\otimes1)=\sum_i v_i\otimes\Delta(a_i).$$
The last expression is $(1\otimes\Delta)c(v)$. This proves coassociativity by equality of the actual tensors in $V\otimes_k(A\otimes_kA)$; no test on field-valued or rational points is used.

source.place: Remark 4.1, printed p.84, necessity of (25), made explicit at the two universal points.

proof.text: Apply the Step 2 formula to $R=k$ and $x=\epsilon$, the identity point of $G(k)$ by [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf]. Since $r_k(\epsilon)=1$, it gives $(1\otimes\epsilon)c(v)=v$ under $V\otimes_kk=V$. This is the counit identity. Steps 2-3 already proved that the two formulas are inverse for all natural endomorphism families. Steps 4-6 and this calculation show that they restrict to inverse bijections between representations and coactions, with exactly the displayed formulas in the statement.

source.place: Remark 4.1, printed p.84, the counit equation in (24) and the one-to-one correspondence.

proof.text: Let $f:V\to W$ be $k$-linear. If $f_Rr_{V,R}(x)=r_{W,R}(x)f_R$ for every $R,x$, evaluate at $R=A,x=\mathrm{id}_A$ and $v\otimes1$ to obtain $(f\otimes1)c_V(v)=c_Wf(v)$. Conversely apply $1\otimes x$ to this identity and multiply by $b\in R$. The Step 3 formula gives $f_Rr_{V,R}(x)(v\otimes b)=r_{W,R}(x)f_R(v\otimes b)$, and pure-tensor generation proves equality of the operators. The base-changed $f_R$ and the tensor maps used here are exactly those specified in [def-weil-module-base-change] and [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product].

source.place: Remark 4.1, printed p.84, coordinate description; compare Remark 4.18, printed p.90, for equivariant maps as comodule maps.

proof.text: Suppose $V$ is finite-dimensional and nonzero. Delete dependent vectors from a finite spanning set, solving each dependence for a vector with nonzero coefficient; this gives a basis of size $n\geq1$ [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace]. Under this basis $V_R=R^n$: the mutually inverse maps send $e_i\otimes b$ to $b$ in coordinate $i$, and $(b_i)$ to $\sum_i e_i\otimes b_i$, by the tensor universal property. Endomorphisms are their matrices of basis images, and automorphisms are invertible matrices. Thus [def-sc-general-linear-group] represents $R\mapsto\operatorname{Aut}_R(V_R)$ by the affine group $\operatorname{GL}(V)=\operatorname{GL}_{n,k}$. Apply [lem-galois-yoneda-fully-faithful] to the category $(k\text{-alg})^{\mathrm{op}}$: a natural map from $\operatorname{Hom}_{k\text{-alg}}(A,-)$ to $\operatorname{Hom}_{k\text{-alg}}(k[\operatorname{GL}(V)],-)$ is uniquely a $k$-algebra map $k[\operatorname{GL}(V)]\to A$. By [def-weil-affine-spectrum] it is a morphism $G\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$ over $k$. Its compatibility with multiplication follows from the group-homomorphism law on all algebra-valued points: $G\times_kG$ is affine by [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra], and the same Yoneda injectivity detects equality of the two multiplication composites. Conversely a group-scheme homomorphism induces natural group homomorphisms on points by composition [def-sc-group-scheme]. This is exactly the finite-dimensional representation notion of [def-wf-algebraic-representations].

source.place: Chapter 4(a), printed p.83, finite-dimensional assertion; Remark 4.1, printed p.84, final paragraph. Representability: Stacks Tag 022W (example-general-linear-group); Yoneda: Tag 001P (lemma-yoneda).

proof.text: When $V=0$, each $V_R$ is zero, since every generating tensor is $0\otimes b=0$. Its automorphism group is the one-element group. The functor of one-element groups is represented by $\operatorname{Spec}k$, since there is exactly one $k$-algebra map $k\to R$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Thus $\operatorname{GL}(0)=\operatorname{Spec}k$, and the unique representation corresponds to the structural group-scheme map $G\to\operatorname{Spec}k$. This verifies the zero-dimensional case without applying the positive-rank convention in [def-sc-general-linear-group].

source.place: Chapter 4(a), printed p.83, finite-dimensional assertion, with the zero-vector-space case written out.

proof.text:
For the trivial action every $r_A(\mathrm{id}_A)$ is the identity, so its coaction is $v\mapsto v\otimes1$. For two representations use the identification
$$(V\otimes_kW)\otimes_kR\ \simeq\ (V\otimes_kR)\otimes_R(W\otimes_kR),\quad(v\otimes w)\otimes b\mapsto(v\otimes1)\otimes_R(w\otimes b).$$
The inverse sends $(v\otimes a)\otimes_R(w\otimes b)$ to $(v\otimes w)\otimes ab$; both maps are well-defined by bilinearity and balancing, and their composites fix the displayed generators [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product, def-weil-module-base-change]. Acting on the two factors defines a natural action: the identity and composition laws follow by applying the laws in each factor to a generating tensor, and the inverse acts by the two inverse operators. For $\alpha:R\to R'$ the identification commutes with $1\otimes\alpha$ on generators, and each factor action is natural, so both composites agree on each $(v\otimes w)\otimes b$. At $R=A,x=\mathrm{id}_A$ its value on $(v\otimes w)\otimes1$ is $\sum_{i,j}(v_i\otimes w_j)\otimes a_ib_j$ by the inverse map above. The established dictionary therefore yields exactly the tensor coaction in the statement, in arbitrary dimension.
